title: Recognising and responding to heat stroke in rabbits
subtitle: What to look for and what to do when a rabbit overheats.
excerpt: Rabbits cannot sweat and have limited ability to cool themselves; they are highly vulnerable to heat stroke at temperatures above 28 degrees Celsius. A rabbit that is sprawled, panting, salivating, or unresponsive in hot weather is in a medical emergency. Quick, calm action can save its life. Prevention in summer is straightforward once the risks are understood.
sourceNotes: RSPCA, Rabbit heat stroke: signs and first aid (2022). British Rabbit Council, Rabbit welfare in hot weather (2023). PDSA, Rabbit heat stroke guide (2023). Meredith Animal Hospital, Rabbit Emergency Care: Heat Stroke (2021). RWAF (Rabbit Welfare Association and Fund), Hot weather rabbit care (2022).

glossaryTerms.definition: A medical emergency caused by the body's core temperature rising to a level that damages tissue and disrupts cellular function. In rabbits, onset can be rapid at temperatures above 28 degrees Celsius, particularly in direct sunlight or confined spaces with poor ventilation.

content.text: Rabbits regulate body temperature through blood flow to their ears and through their environment. They cannot pant effectively and do not sweat. In warm weather, an outdoor hutch in direct sunlight or a poorly ventilated shed can push the air temperature to a level that is rapidly fatal.
Heat stroke
kills rabbits quickly and with little warning in some cases.
Signs of overheating
Rapid, shallow breathing or open-mouth breathing with the head raised and neck extended (rabbits do not normally breathe through their mouths).
Wet or glistening fur around the mouth, ears, and nose from excessive salivation.
Bright red or pale ear flaps, the ears normally appear pink; very red or mottled ears indicate circulatory stress.
Sprawled flat with limbs extended and no reaction to being approached: a rabbit in collapse.
Seizures in severe cases.
Immediate response
Move the rabbit immediately to the coolest available environment: a shaded, ventilated indoor space. Do not leave it outside even in shade, the ambient air temperature is the problem.

Dampen the ears and feet with cool (not cold or iced) water. The ears are the primary heat exchange surface; cooling them directly draws heat from the blood supply. Do not submerge the rabbit or pour cold water over the body: sudden cold causes shock.
Place the rabbit on a cool, damp towel. A ceramic tile from the freezer, wrapped in a thin cloth, under the rabbit's body works well.
Offer water but do not force the rabbit to drink. A rabbit in heat stroke may not be able to swallow reliably.
Call a vet immediately. A rabbit showing signs of heat stroke needs veterinary assessment even if it appears to recover: organ damage from heat stroke can cause death hours after the initial episode.
Prevention in summer
Move hutches out of direct sunlight from May onwards. A hutch against a south-facing wall in July can reach fatal temperatures in two hours of direct sun.
Provide ceramic tiles, marble offcuts, or a cold water bottle wrapped in a towel in the hutch for the rabbit to lie against.
Ensure the hutch or run has through-ventilation rather than just one opening, so air moves across the rabbit rather than pooling.
Check on rabbits at the hottest part of the day (typically 1 to 4 pm) rather than just morning and evening.

attrs.cue: Rabbit appears to recover after cooling but is still lethargic and off food the next day
attrs.cause: Internal organ stress or early kidney damage from the heat episode
attrs.fix: Vet visit. Post-heat-stroke organ damage is not visible from the outside and a blood panel can identify it before it becomes a crisis.
